title: The Late Cipher
premise: Rafael Thackeray, a retired detective hiding behind a failing bookshop and a carefully erased past, is pulled back into the world he fled when a corpse wearing his own clothes surfaces in the canal. The dead man is a stranger with Rafael's face on a decades-old photograph, and the only clue is a cipher ledger hidden in the shop's inventory, encoded by the partner whose death Rafael staged to survive. As a relentless inspector closes in and old enemies realize the witness they buried is alive, Rafael must decode the ledger to expose the corruption ring that once owned him. In the end, Rafael trades his invisibility for justice, testifying at last and accepting that survival bought with silence was never really living.
about_author: W. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former forensic archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing cold cases before turning to fiction. They write from a coastal town where fog is frequent and alibis are thin.

chapters.title: The Body Wore My Coat
chapters.summary: Rafael Thackeray's POV. Opening the bookshop on a gray morning, Rafael is summoned to the canal where police have pulled out a man dressed head-to-toe in clothes stolen from Rafael's own closet, down to a monogrammed cufflink. The shock cracks his careful invisibility; the emotional beat is dread—the past has found an address.

chapters.title: Inventory of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He inventories the shop and discovers one shelf of books subtly reordered—spines forming a pattern he almost recognizes. Detective Inspector Sorrel Vane arrives with questions about the victim, whom no one can identify. Beat: paranoia sharpening into purpose as Rafael realizes the arrangement is deliberate.

chapters.title: A Stranger With My Face
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Among the dead man's effects is a photograph: two young men, one unmistakably Rafael thirty years ago, the other a stranger who looks enough like him to be kin. Flashback fragments surface unbidden. Beat: grief and guilt—memory returning like floodwater through a cracked seal.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Deciphering the shelf order, Rafael finds numbers penciled inside dust jackets—a ledger of payments, dates, initials. It matches nothing he remembers until he finds his dead partner Ellery's handwriting. Beat: vertigo; the friend he mourned may have been keeping accounts of their sins.

chapters.title: Inspector Vane
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Sorrel Vane interviews Rafael, noting his composure is too practiced for a civilian. She pulls his sealed personnel file and finds a twenty-year gap. Beat: cat-and-mouse tension; she suspects him of everything and respects him for it.

chapters.title: What Ellery Knew
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Digging through a storage unit, Rafael recovers Ellery's hidden notebook: proof that their old unit took bribes from the Marrow family syndicate, and that Ellery planned to testify before dying in the 'accident' Rafael helped stage—or did he? Beat: dawning horror that his survival was engineered by someone else.

chapters.title: The Second Copy
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane discovers the canal victim had a key to a locker containing photographs of Rafael's old team—and a train ticket dated the day after his death. Someone expected the man to leave alive. Beat: her suspicion pivots from Rafael toward a larger design.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Missing
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael identifies the victim via dental records: Tomas Reyes, a minor fixer for the Marrows who once served as his body double during surveillance ops. Why would Tomas wear his clothes to die? Beat: cold clarity—Tomas wasn't impersonating Rafael; he was warning him.

chapters.title: Old Debts
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A threatening note arrives tucked into a returned book: 'The ledger balances either way.' Rafael realizes the Marrows' surviving lieutenant, Corvus Hale, knows he's alive. Beat: fear curdling into defiance—he decides to finish decoding rather than run.

chapters.title: The Cipher's Key
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Working nights, Rafael cracks the substitution scheme: the key phrase is a line from a poem Ellery annotated in the margins of every book they sold together. The ledger names payees—including a judge, a councilman, and one initial R.T. marked 'owed.' Beat: shame; he was on the list all along.

chapters.title: Vane's Gap
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane confronts Rafael with the file gap and offers a deal: full confession for protection. Rafael refuses, showing her only the ledger's existence, not its contents. Beat: uneasy alliance forming—two people who both distrust the institutions they serve.

chapters.title: The Bookshop Burns
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Arson destroys the shop overnight; the ledger shelf survives because Rafael moved it days earlier, suspecting surveillance. Watching his refuge burn, he feels strangely lighter. Beat: liberation through loss—invisibility was the cage, not the shelter.

chapters.title: Hale's Invitation
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Corvus Hale summons Rafael to a marina meeting, offering money and exile in exchange for the ledger, revealing that Ellery didn't die in the accident—he was executed after Rafael fled, and the 'accident' was cover. Beat: devastating guilt reframed; his escape cost his friend everything.

chapters.title: What Rafael Owed
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Re-reading the ledger's final entries, Rafael decodes a message Ellery embedded for him personally: instructions to a safe deposit box and the words 'finish it for both of us.' Beat: resolve hardening into vow; grief converted to mission.

chapters.title: The Deposit Box
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane tails Rafael to the bank and witnesses him retrieve recordings Ellery made before his death—confessions implicating Hale and the judge. Instead of arresting Rafael, she pockets her warrant. Beat: trust extended against protocol; her career now staked on him.

chapters.title: Double Exposure
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The recordings reveal why Tomas died: he was hired to impersonate Rafael at a handoff, then eliminated as loose ends. Hale planned to resurrect 'Rafael Thackeray' as a scapegoat for the syndicate's crimes. Beat: icy anger—the frame was always meant to close around him.

chapters.title: The Trap They Built for Me
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rather than flee, Rafael lets Hale believe he's taking the deal, feeding him a forged ledger copy through a middleman. Vane coordinates quietly, against orders. Beat: tense agency—the hunted man setting the snare.

chapters.title: Marina, Midnight
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The handoff goes wrong when Hale brings reinforcements; Rafael is captured aboard Hale's boat while Vane loses visual. Beat: climax rising—Rafael face-to-face with the man who ordered Ellery's death, buying time with talk while Vane races the tide.

chapters.title: The Confession Recording
chapters.summary: Climax. Rafael provokes Hale into confessing to Ellery's murder and Tomas's, knowing Vane's wire is recording from the docked tender below. Gunfire, a struggle, and Vane's team storms the boat. Beat: catharsis—the truth spoken aloud at last, costing blood but not lives.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael takes the stand, surrendering his own sealed crimes alongside the syndicate's, accepting charges for obstruction in exchange for cooperation. Beat: costly redemption—justice that includes himself, no clean exits.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane watches the verdicts: Hale convicted, Rafael sentenced to community service and probation, his detective's pension forfeited. She visits him after, neither quite friend nor adversary. Beat: quiet respect between two people rebuilt by the same case.

chapters.title: Shelf Life
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Months later, Rafael reopens a smaller bookshop under his real name for the first time in decades, shelving Ellery's poem-facedition where customers can find it. A young officer buys a mystery novel and asks if he was ever a detective. 'Once,' he says. Beat: peace earned, identity reclaimed—visible at last, and unafraid.
